ATGE should be treated primarily as a demand anchor/customer/operator for online and hybrid healthcare education infrastructure, not as a supplier pure-play.

Need a follow-up pass for delisted/private and recently distressed OPM peers, LMS/SIS vendors, enrollment marketing agencies, payment processors, proctoring/testing vendors, and clinical placement software providers; this pass stayed limited to direct US-listed public candidates.

Online higher education fixed-cost intensity is supported by evidence around recruitment, student services, course development, national marketing, and student-information systems; this justifies searching beyond obvious content platforms.

NNI is an underfollowed candidate to investigate for education technology services, payments, loan servicing systems, software, subscriptions, and student lifecycle workflows.

Public-market coverage of pure student-information systems and online program management suppliers is limited because several obvious platforms may be private, acquired, or embedded in broader enterprise software companies; later layers should verify current listings before inclusion.
Simulation and VR equipment for healthcare education is a potential scarce capacity-enabler, but current evidence only supports the category, not a confirmed CAE customer link.

LOPE is the cleanest direct public-market mapping for the online higher-education fixed-cost stack because it explicitly provides enrollment, student services, SIS support, marketing, curriculum, and faculty support to university partners.

NNI should be tracked as an underfollowed infrastructure candidate because its loan-servicing identity may obscure education technology, payments, financial management, and student/school information system exposure.

COUR belongs in the universe as a platform and credential-distribution layer, but later layers must distinguish durable university infrastructure revenue from consumer course demand and lower-retention enterprise revenue.

LRN is a speculative-shadow candidate for this specific node: strong online learning/career-learning relevance, but higher-education fixed-cost-stack exposure is less direct and must be verified by segment and customer evidence.
The node appears investable through service-stack providers, education payments/SIS vendors, credential platforms, and online career-learning operators rather than through universities alone.

Many true SIS, LMS, and OPM assets are private or recently taken private; later passes should check whether any public micro/small-cap vendors remain in niche admissions CRM, proctoring, accreditation, simulation labs, or healthcare education workflow software.

The online-program fixed-cost stack includes recruitment, student services, course development, national marketing, and student-information systems; these costs are incurred before tuition revenue and can create chokepoint-like advantages for scaled vendors or institutions.
